content:
# Workshop 9
 
 # Listening to the Public with AI
 
 **Speakers:** [Beth Goldberg](https:/www.linkedin.com/in/-bethgoldberg) (Head of Research and Development, Jigsaw) and [Ben Peterson](https:/www.linkedin.com/in/ben-peterson-61330043) (Executive Director, Bowling Green City-County Planning Commission)
 
 Bowling Green, Kentucky, is facing rapid growth and wants to decide whether that growth would "happen to us or for us,” in the words of the Warren County Judge/Executive. Traditional participation mechanisms gave planners highly skewed input from the loudest voices rather than a broad picture of community priorities. Traditional town halls attracted only about 8 people, and Peterson noted that "the normal process has become less effective; it can feel like the loudest and most belligerent people win."
 
 The speakers discuss how Bowling Green used an AI-enabled, community-led process to engage residents at scale about the city's future.
 
 ### The partnership and approach
 
 Local government (the Warren County Planning Commission), Jigsaw (Google's technology incubator), and Innovation Engine (a local civil society group) formed a partnership to design and deliver the engagement.
 
 The team started by visiting residents at their homes across Bowling Green to understand their perspectives on civic participation. The biggest barrier turned out not to be mistrust of local government but low self-efficacy. People didn't believe they knew enough to contribute to civic spaces and felt unsure whether they belonged.
 
 The project responded by building a network of 80-100 "listening partners" (community leaders from diverse sectors, ages, and backgrounds) who co-designed everything from outreach materials to the final report format. These partners then became ambassadors, using hyper-local, multilingual outreach through trusted channels, such as QR codes in mosques and churches, WhatsApp groups, basketball games, coffee shops, and local media partnerships.
 
 The effort was government-sanctioned (giving it legitimacy) but not government-fronted (building trust through community voices).
 
 ### 
 
 ### Technology stack
 
 The digital engagement used [Pol.is](http:/pol.is) , an open source platform used to convene online dialogues with groups. The engagement presented participants with one open-ended question:
 
 "What do you hope to see in Bowling Green's future? What do you hope to preserve?"
 
 Participants were then shown others’ statements. They could respond with short comments and vote on whether to agree or disagree with others' statements.
 
 The interface was mobile-first, anonymous, required no login, and took just minutes to complete. [Perspective API](https:/perspectiveapi.com) ran in the background to filter toxic content.
 
 After the engagement closed, [Jigsaw's Sensemaker tool](https:/jigsaw-code.github.io/sensemaking-tools) (powered by Google's Gemini LLM) categorized comments into topics and subtopics, synthesized clusters into summaries without erasing "spicier" views or minority perspectives, and identified common ground where diverse language pointed to the same underlying idea (e.g., open space for both hunting and hiking).
 
 #### 
 
 ### Results and impact
 
 The engagement launched in February 2024 and was open for 33 days. Nearly 8,000 people participated (over 10% of Bowling Green’s population), generating 4,000+ proposals and over a million votes.
 
 Survey evidence showed 83% of participants reported better understanding of different viewpoints, and local officials reported feeling more confident they could accurately represent the community. As Beth Goldberg emphasized: "The AI piece is about two percent of the whole process; the rest is community-wide collaboration and co-ownership."
 
 #### 
 
 ### Turning data into policy
 
 After the 33-day engagement period closed, Jigsaw’s Sensemaker tool, powered by Google’s Gemini LLM, processed the proposals and votes in minutes. The tool [produced a comprehensive, interactive public report](https:/report.whatcouldbgbe.com) that became the primary output of the engagement process.
 
 The report featured:
 
 (1) Topic-level summaries organized into 12 major categories (Arts & Culture, Infrastructure & Transportation, Housing, etc.) with 70 subtopics.
 
 (2) An interactive data explorer allowing users to filter by topic, sort by consensus level, and search specific ideas.
 
 (3) “Highlights” section identifying proposals with high consensus (over 2,370 ideas had 80%+ agreement).
 
 (4) Visual design that was accessible and engaging, featuring local imagery and branding.
 
 The report was designed in collaboration with the community listening partners to ensure it was actionable for decision-makers while remaining accessible to the public. All underlying data were made publicly available so that community members, businesses, and nonprofits could also act on the findings.
 
 Bowling Green is now using results in two parallel tracks:
 
 (1) County/City track: Thec community listening partners are reviewing results and submitting top 10 priorities per category to a steering committee of local officials
 
 (2) Planning Commission track: Using growth-related comments (housing, transportation, infrastructure) as a foundation for a new BG2050 comprehensive plan
 
 Peterson described the process as a funnel: "We started very broad. Now we're narrowing this down further and putting this process and feedback loop to work to keep refining as we get more specific." According to surveys Jigsaw conducted, the AI saved local leaders an average of 28 work days, and 83% of surveyed residents believed the report would lead to a better plan for Bowling Green’s future.
 
 ## 
 
 ## Project metrics
 
 | Population | ~70,000 (Bowling Green city) |
 |------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
 | Participation | 8,000+ people (>10% of population) |
 | Traditional comparison | ~8 people at recent town halls |
 | Proposals generated | 4,000+ |
 | Votes cast | 1 million+ |
 | Timeline | ~1 month of active engagement |
 | Listening partners | 80-100 community leaders |
 | Gov't staff time | Primarily 1 person (Ben Peterson) + 80-100 community volunteers |
 | Post-engagement impact | 83% of residents reported a better understanding of different viewpoints 83% of residents believed the report would lead to a better plan for Bowling Green’s future 96% of leaders felt the report made it easier to solicit input from the community on its future 98% of leaders felt the report made it easier to share key takeaways with residents |
 | | |
 
 ## Takeaways for learners
 
 AI is for sense-making, not a replacement for the hard work of engagement. The Sensemaker tool helped to draw insights from a large volume of public comments, essentially streamlining the last 2% of the work. The hard work was designing a process and getting people to show up.
 
 Human infrastructure was central to engagement. The listening partners network, local media collaborations, and highly local physical placement of QR codes boosted engagement. This is a place-specific organizing story with digital tools layered on top.
 
 Start from the end goal and design the question accordingly. Bowling Green's aim was to generate a vision and priorities for growth. That justified one broad, future-oriented prompt. If you need concrete options or decisions, you would design a different structure.
 
 Relatedly, some of the design tradeoffs and tensions present: open vs representative (they chose to push participation and do a separate representative survey later); anonymity vs accountability (chose anonymity for safety/honesty); broad vs narrow questions (one open question generates ideas but not decisions); short vs long engagement (quick, text-only format kept it brief and focused on substance).
 
 Low self-efficacy is a significant barrier to engagement. People stayed away because they felt unqualified or unwelcome, not because they hated local government. This has direct implications for course content: emphasize lived experience as expertise, and design exercises that reduce psychological as well as logistical barriers to participation.
 
 ## Audience notes
 
 ### Questions
 
 “Can local government run this without Jigsaw?” (Answer: Somewhat, tools are open-source, but "open-source" doesn't mean "easy off-the-shelf,” and this does require technical capacity)
 
 “How much staff time was required?”
 
 “What marketing/design resources are needed?” (Significant investment in multilingual materials, local media partnerships)
 
 “Was the LLM fine-tuned or just prompted?” (Implied: mostly prompting, with iteration to preserve "spicy" minority views)
 
 “Can demographic data be collected without compromising anonymity?”
 
 “How to prevent bot or non-resident participation?”
 
 “How to reach people without broadband, English fluency, or trust in technology?”
 
 “How to ‘close the loop’ and show residents their input mattered?”
 
 “How to sustain this kind of engagement beyond one-off projects?”
 
 ### 
 
 ## Quotes
 
 ### Beth Goldberg (Jigsaw/Google)
 
 "People needed to be invited in by people they trusted, and they needed to know their time was going to be worthwhile."
 
 "It wasn't that people mistrusted local government; the biggest barrier was low self-efficacy."
 
 "Large language models helped us categorize, synthesize without losing nuance, and find common ground across thousands of comments."
 
 "The AI piece is about two percent of the whole process; the rest is community-wide collaboration and co-ownership."
 
 "Don't let AI intimidation or fear of hallucination be the gating factor here."
 
 ### Ben Peterson (Warren County/Bowling Green)
 
 "We had nothing to lose. Traditional processes weren't working anymore, especially post-COVID."
 
 "The normal process has become less effective; it can feel like the loudest and most belligerent people win."
 
 "As government officials, we often only hear the complaints. We don't always hear anything reaffirming that we're doing things right."
 
 "You can't do this on your own—it really has to be a community effort with the doers in your community leading."
 
 ### Doug Gorman (Judge Executive, quoted by Beth G.)
 
 "Do we want this growth to happen to us, or do we want it to happen for us?"
 
 ### 
 
 ## Platforms/Tools/Resources
 
 [Pol.is](http:/pol.is) – A core digital conversation platform used to collect free-text statements and agree/disagree votes at scale. Also used for vTaiwan.
 
 ["What Could BG Be?" public engagement site](https:/www.whatcouldbgbe.com)
 
 [Jigsaw Sensemaker / Sensemaking Tools](https:/jigsaw-code.github.io/sensemaking-tools) – Open-source suite used to cluster comments into topics and subtopics, generate topic-level summaries, surface areas of agreement/disagreement and "common ground."
 
 [Perspective API – Comment-moderation tool used in the background to filter toxic content and keep dialogue civil.](https:/perspectiveapi.com)
 
 [Jigsaw Bowling Green case study: "How one of the fastest-growing cities in Kentucky used AI to plan for the next 25 years."](https:/medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd1412)
 
 [Jigsaw research note on facilitator-informed design of AI tools for collective deliberation](https:/medium.com/jigsaw/building-better-dialogue-tools-5ff8fe3de9f9)
 
 [BG 2050 project narrative: "Civic imagination meets AI: how Bowling Green is creatively preparing for rapid growth."](https:/www.kentuckytotheworld.org/blog/civic-imagination-meets-ai-how-bowling-green-is-creatively-preparing-for-rapid-growth)
 
 [We the People](https:/freedom.wethepeople-250.org) – Jigsaw's follow-up at the national scale with methodological advances: representative recruitment from every congressional district; three-round process; 1.6 million words of input into 26 sentence-long statements; questions focused on values/ideals, not policy specifics.
 
 [USC Civic Imagination Project](https:/www.civicimaginationproject.org) – Framework used by Innovation Engine in the BG2050 work:
 
 [Innovation Engine overview of the civic imagination method](https:/www.innoengine.co/civic-imagination)
